opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a reasonable concern to take seriously, but in most cases I think people overweight it. Machine learning is a huge field now. There are tens of thousands of researchers and engineers working on it, and an enormous amount of commercial money pushing it forward. So if you're one more person joining, the marginal effect you have on how fast the overall field moves is pretty small. The field doesn't really hinge on any one individual.

What you get in return can be quite large. You build real skills: you learn how to train models, how to run experiments, and you develop intuitions about what these systems actually do, as opposed to what people speculate they do. If you then want to work on alignment, that experience is extremely valuable. A lot of the most useful alignment work right now is empirical, and you need people who are good ML practitioners to do it. Some of the bottleneck in alignment is simply having enough people who can do that work well.

That said, I don't think it's a blanket "don't worry about it." It depends a lot on what you're working on. If your job is to push the frontier of capabilities in some significant way, like scaling up the biggest models or finding the next big algorithmic trick, then the acceleration concern is much more real, and you should think hard about whether that's the right thing for you to do. If you're doing more applied work, or something that builds skills without moving the frontier much, I'd worry a lot less.

I'd also think about where you go. Working at a place that takes safety seriously, where you can influence culture and norms, and where there's a path toward safety work, is different from going somewhere that doesn't care at all. And be honest with yourself about whether you'll actually make the switch to safety later, because it's easy to tell yourself you'll do it and then stay where you are.

So overall: the acceleration cost is usually small and the career capital is usually substantial, but look at the specifics of the role rather than treating all ML jobs the same.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people often overweight the acceleration concern, while the career capital from ML work is substantial.

r002.rationale: It recommends building ML skills and experience that are valuable for a later move into empirical alignment work.

r003.rationale: The candidate says one more person has little effect on the pace of the overall ML field and that alignment needs skilled practitioners, but does not clearly argue that an individual would make a larger marginal difference in alignment than in capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a worry a lot of people have, and I take it seriously, but I think it's mostly overstated — at least for the kind of roles we're talking about.

The first thing to say is that the marginal effect of any single person is pretty small. Machine learning as a field is huge and growing fast, there are thousands of very talented people going into it, and there's an enormous amount of commercial pressure driving capabilities forward. If you decide not to take a job at a lab, that position gets filled by someone else, probably someone who isn't thinking about these risks at all. So the counterfactual impact on timelines is really marginal, whereas the counterfactual impact on safety can be quite large, because the pool of people who actually care about this and have the technical skills to do something about it is still very small.

The second point is that I think the distinction between "capabilities work" and "safety work" is blurrier than people sometimes make it out to be. A lot of what I'd consider alignment research — things like learning from human feedback, reward modelling, interpretability — these require you to deeply understand how the models work, and they often require you to be at a place that has access to frontier models. You can't really do this work well in isolation. And some of it does incidentally make models more useful, which is fine; I think that's a feature, not a bug, because it means the safety techniques actually get deployed.

That said, I do think there's a real version of the concern. If your job is purely about scaling things up faster, finding the next big architecture, and you're not doing anything to make the systems more aligned or more understood, then yeah, you should think hard about whether that's the best use of your career. And I think people should be honest with themselves about that rather than telling themselves a story about how they're "influencing the culture from the inside."

But my overall take is: if you have the skills, go work on alignment. Do it at a place where you can be close to the frontier, because that's where the problems actually show up and that's where the solutions need to be built. The thing we need most right now is more good people working on the problem, not fewer people working in ML.

r001.rationale: It says a person's effect on timelines is small, but does not discuss career capital gained from an ML job.

r002.rationale: It recommends working on alignment near the frontier, but does not present ML work as a way to build skills for a later transition into alignment.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the small marginal timeline impact of one person with a potentially large safety impact, citing the small pool of technically skilled people who care about alignment.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a legitimate concern, but it depends a lot on what you’d actually be doing. Machine learning is a very broad field. Working on making general-purpose systems more capable has a different effect from working on how to evaluate whether those systems are safe, or how to make them easier to oversee.

There’s also a tradeoff here: if you want to do useful technical alignment work, you need to understand machine learning. Getting practical experience can make you much more effective at that. So I wouldn’t want people to conclude that they should avoid learning these skills because they might contribute to progress along the way.

The question I’d ask is: what does this particular job let you contribute, and where does it put you in a few years? Are you developing skills that are useful for safety? Are there people you can learn from? Is there a realistic path to working directly on alignment? And how much would your work actually accelerate capabilities compared with what would happen without you?

I don’t think there’s a blanket answer that taking a machine learning job is good or bad. But I do think it’s worth being deliberate about which problems you work on, rather than assuming that any machine learning experience will eventually translate into a positive impact.

r001.rationale: The response calls the concern legitimate and weighs it against the value of practical experience, but does not argue that the concern undervalues career capital.

r002.rationale: It says practical machine learning experience can make someone more effective at technical alignment and asks whether a job offers a path to working directly on alignment.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes capabilities work from safety work and asks about a job’s effect, but does not argue that an additional person makes a larger marginal difference in alignment than in capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a legitimate concern. If you work on improving the capabilities of AI systems, some of your contribution could bring forward the point where we have very powerful AI. And if we’re not prepared for that, that could be harmful.

But I wouldn’t treat all machine learning jobs as equivalent. The important question is what you would actually be working on. Would you be helping us understand and control these systems, or mainly making them more capable? There are also benefits to learning the field: if you want to do technical safety research, you need to understand machine learning, and practical experience can be valuable.

So I’d think about the particular role, the team, and what opportunities it gives you to work on safety. I don’t think ‘never take a machine learning job’ is a good general rule. But neither is ‘anything that gives you machine learning experience is good.’ You have to look at the work itself and ask what difference you’re likely to make.

r001.rationale: The response says machine learning experience can be valuable for safety research, but does not argue that this benefit is undervalued by the concern about accelerating timelines.

r002.rationale: It says practical machine learning experience is valuable because technical safety researchers need to understand machine learning, communicating it as preparation for safety work.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes safety-focused work from capability work, but does not argue that an additional person would make a larger marginal difference in alignment than in capabilities.
